fix-flip-profit.formula: selling = ARV x sell%; all_in = purchase + rehab + holding + financing + selling; profit = ARV - all_in; margin = profit/ARV; roi = profit/cash; annual = roi x 12/months.
fix-flip-profit.edition: The fix-and-flip profit and return computation used by real-estate investors, by name.
fix-flip-profit.freeAccess: The all-in-cost, profit, and cash-return breakdown of a flip is a widely-published real-estate-investing computation.
fix-flip-profit.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
fix-flip-profit.editionNote: Fix-and-flip profit: the all-in cost = purchase + rehab + holding + financing + selling costs (selling = ARV x selling%), the net profit = ARV - all-in, and the returns are profit / ARV (the margin), profit / cash invested (the cash-on-cash ROI), and that annualized over the hold (x 12 / months). This screens a deal from the entered figures; the ARV must come from real comparable sales and the rehab from a real scope, and it does not model the tax on the gain or the risk of an ARV miss or rehab overrun. A screening aid; the actual deal and a professional's numbers govern.

assumptions.name: All-in cost
assumptions.value: purchase + rehab + holding + financing + selling (ARV x sell%)

assumptions.name: Returns
assumptions.value: margin = profit/ARV, cash ROI = profit/cash, annualized x 12/months

assumptions.name: Unverified inputs
assumptions.value: ARV from real comps, rehab from a real scope; gain tax not modeled

floor-area-ratio.formula: FAR = building_floor_area / lot_area; max_buildable = FAR_limit x lot_area; remaining = max_buildable - existing_floor_area.
floor-area-ratio.edition: Floor area ratio, the municipal zoning intensity measure, by name; the zoning ordinance and planning authority govern.
floor-area-ratio.freeAccess: FAR is a standard zoning ratio; the floor area and lot area come from the survey and the local zoning code's definition of countable floor area.
floor-area-ratio.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
floor-area-ratio.editionNote: Floor area ratio (FAR) = gross building floor area / lot area, the standard zoning measure of building intensity. A FAR of 1.0 is a building whose floor area equals the lot area (one story over the whole lot, two over half), so FAR caps bulk without dictating footprint or height. Where a limit is set, the maximum buildable floor area = FAR_limit x lot area and the remaining capacity is that minus the existing floor area. What counts as floor area -- whether parking, basements, mechanical space, and balconies are included -- varies by municipality, so enter the gross figure the local code defines as countable. A screening aid, not a zoning determination; the ordinance, its exclusions, and the planning authority govern.

assumptions.name: Countable floor area varies
assumptions.value: municipalities differ on whether parking, basements, and mechanical space count; enter the locally-defined gross figure

assumptions.name: Max buildable
assumptions.value: maximum buildable floor area = FAR_limit x lot area

doubling-time.formula: Td = elapsed x ln(2) / ln(N / N0); mu = ln(N / N0) / elapsed; doublings = log2(N / N0).
doubling-time.edition: Exponential-growth / population-doubling kinetics (standard growth analysis), by name.
doubling-time.freeAccess: Standard microbiology / cell-culture growth-kinetics relation; the culture and conditions govern.
doubling-time.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
doubling-time.editionNote: Doubling time is constant only during log (exponential) phase, so a measurement spanning lag or stationary phase is meaningless; if N is an optical density the ratio assumes OD stays proportional to cell count (which fails at high density). An analysis aid, not a validated growth assay.

assumptions.name: Growth phase
assumptions.value: valid only during log (exponential) phase; lag / stationary spans are meaningless

grain-drying-energy.formula: weight = bushels x lb/bu; water = weight x (Mi - Mf)/(100 - Mf); energy = water x Btu/lb; propane = energy / 91500.
grain-drying-energy.edition: Grain drying energy from the wet-basis shrink and a heat balance, standard grain-handling practice, by name.
grain-drying-energy.freeAccess: The wet-basis moisture-shrink formula and the propane heat content (91,500 Btu/gal) are public grain-handling results.
grain-drying-energy.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
grain-drying-energy.editionNote: Grain drying energy: the weight = bushels x the test weight (lb/bushel), the water removed = weight x (Mi - Mf)/(100 - Mf) on the wet basis (the standard shrink formula, where the denominator shifts because the dry matter is conserved), the drying energy = water x the per-pound energy (commonly about 1500 Btu/lb including dryer efficiency, well above the 970 Btu/lb latent heat), and the propane = energy / 91,500 Btu per gallon. Each moisture point removed nearer the wet end carries slightly more water. This estimates the energy and fuel; the dryer's actual efficiency, the fuel's heat content, and the elevator's discount/shrink schedule govern.

assumptions.name: Water removed
assumptions.value: weight x (Mi - Mf)/(100 - Mf), wet basis

assumptions.name: Energy and fuel
assumptions.value: energy = water x ~1500 Btu/lb; propane = energy / 91500 Btu/gal

assumptions.name: Efficiency
assumptions.value: the ~1500 Btu/lb includes dryer efficiency; actual varies

poe-budget.formula: I = pse_W / V_source; loop resistance R = R_per_100m × (L / 100m) × (1 + α × (T − 20°C)); P_loss = I² × R, with R halved for 802.3bt Type 3 / 4 (power on all four pairs, two pair-sets in parallel); V_source 44 V (af), 50 V (at, bt3), 52 V (bt4); PD power = pse_W − P_loss; flagged against IEEE 802.3 class minimums.
poe-budget.edition: IEEE 802.3bt-2018 by name; manufacturer category cable resistance (Belden / CommScope) attributed in shard.
poe-budget.freeAccess: IEEE 802.3 free at standards.ieee.org/getieee802. Cable specs free at each manufacturer site.
poe-budget.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.

coagulant-dose.formula: pure_lb_day = flow_MGD × jar_dose_mg_L × 8.34 (mass-balance constant for water). product_lb_day = pure_lb_day / (strength_pct / 100). product_gal_day = product_lb_day / (sg × 8.34).
coagulant-dose.edition: Metcalf & Eddy (Wastewater Engineering: Treatment and Resource Recovery, 5th ed.) by name; AWWA M37 (Operational Control of Coagulation and Filtration Processes) by name. Manufacturer product-strength + density values (alum 48.5% sg 1.33, ferric chloride 38% sg 1.40, PAC 10% sg 1.20).
coagulant-dose.freeAccess: Metcalf & Eddy / AWWA M37 licensed; jar-test methodology free in EPA SDWA training materials at epa.gov.
coagulant-dose.governance: Estimate. Operator of record and primacy agency govern.
coagulant-dose.editionNote: Single-edition (engineering-practice constant + manufacturer product strengths; quarterly recheck of manufacturer attribution).

assumptions.name: Constant 8.34 lb/gal
assumptions.value: water at 60 °F

assumptions.name: Product strengths
assumptions.value: alum dry 100%, alum liquid 48.5%, ferric chloride 38%, PAC 10%

assumptions.name: Product specific gravities
assumptions.value: alum liquid 1.33, ferric 1.40, PAC 1.20

bifacial-pv-gain.formula: bifacial_gain = bifaciality x (rear_poa_wm2 / front_poa_wm2); bifacial_gain_pct = 100 x bifacial_gain; effective_power_w = front_power_w x (1 + bifacial_gain).
bifacial-pv-gain.edition: Bifacial PV rear-side gain (bifaciality-coefficient effective-irradiance model), by name; the module datasheet bifaciality, the site albedo and rear-shading, and a bifacial ray-trace (PVsyst / NREL) govern the yield.
bifacial-pv-gain.freeAccess: The bifacial effective-irradiance relation is public PV engineering practice; the bifaciality coefficient is on the module datasheet and the rear irradiance comes from a site model.
bifacial-pv-gain.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
bifacial-pv-gain.editionNote: A bifacial photovoltaic module collects light on both faces: the front makes power the ordinary way, and the back cells make additional power from light reflected up onto them from the ground or roof. The back is less efficient than the front, and the datasheet captures that with the bifaciality coefficient (phi), the ratio of rear to front efficiency -- typically 0.65 to 0.90 for modern cells. The extra output relative to a front-only module is simply phi times the ratio of rear-side to front-side plane-of-array irradiance. A module with phi = 0.75 whose back sees 150 W/m^2 while its front sees 1000 W/m^2 gains 0.75 x 0.15 = 0.1125, or 11.25%, so a 400 W front nameplate becomes about 445 W effective. What drives the rear irradiance is the site, not the module: it rises with a higher ground albedo (a white membrane or light gravel reflects roughly 0.5 to 0.7 of incident light versus about 0.1 for dark asphalt), a taller mounting height that lets more reflected light reach the back, wider row spacing, and less shading from the rack and structure behind the module. Over a bright white roof the same module might see 250 W/m^2 on the back, a gain of 18.75% and about 475 W. This is a first-order yield estimate; the module datasheet's bifaciality, the actual measured or modeled site albedo and rear-side shading, and a proper bifacial ray-trace (as in PVsyst or NREL's bifacial model) govern the real energy, and the inverter and conductors must still be sized for the boosted output.

assumptions.name: Bifacial effective irradiance
assumptions.value: gain = bifaciality x (rear POA / front POA); effective power = front x (1 + gain)

assumptions.name: Bifaciality and albedo
assumptions.value: phi ~0.65-0.90 from the datasheet; rear POA rises with ground albedo (white membrane ~0.5-0.7 vs asphalt ~0.1), mount height, and row spacing

ev-load-management-ems.formula: unmanaged_sum = 1.25 x per_charger x count; managed_demand = evems_limit > 0 ? (setpoint125 ? 1.25 : 1.0) x evems_limit : unmanaged_sum; freed_headroom = unmanaged_sum - managed_demand.
ev-load-management-ems.edition: NEC 2023 (NFPA 70). Article 625 (625.42(A) energy management systems) with the 2026 625.48 continuous factor on the EVEMS setpoint.
ev-load-management-ems.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
ev-load-management-ems.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow NEC 2023. NEC 2026 is the current published edition; jurisdictions on NEC 2017 / 2020 / 2023 / 2026 use slightly different ambient corrections and ampacity ranges; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: Diversified demand
assumptions.value: with a listed EVEMS the demand is the aggregate limit it enforces, not the sum of all chargers at 125%

assumptions.name: 2026 setpoint factor
assumptions.value: the 2026 NEC (625.48) applies the 125% continuous factor to the EVEMS setpoint; the EVEMS must be listed and enforced in hardware

service-load-standard.formula: Standard Method per NEC 2023 Table 220.45 (general lighting demand factors, 220.42 before 2023: first 3000 VA at 100%, next 117000 VA at 35%, remainder at 25%); 220.53 (fixed appliances 75% where four or more fastened-in-place appliances share the feeder or service); 220.54 (dryer 5000 W or nameplate, whichever is greater); 220.55 (range simplified); 430.24 (largest motor at 125%); 220.60 (HVAC larger of cooling vs. heating). Service A = total_VA / V; recommended service from the NEC 100/125/150/175/200/225/300/400 ladder.
service-load-standard.edition: NEC 2023 (NFPA 70). Article 220 (Branch-Circuit, Feeder, and Service Load Calculations).
service-load-standard.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
service-load-standard.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow NEC 2023. NEC 2026 is the current published edition; jurisdictions on NEC 2017 / 2020 / 2023 / 2026 use slightly different ambient corrections and ampacity ranges; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: General lighting load density
assumptions.value: 3 VA per ft² (NEC 2023 220.41 dwelling)

assumptions.name: Small-appliance circuit value
assumptions.value: 1500 VA per circuit (≥ 2 required)

assumptions.name: Laundry circuit value
assumptions.value: 1500 VA (one required)

assumptions.name: Service voltage
assumptions.value: 240 V single-phase split unless user supplies

manning-slope.formula: English Manning V = (1.486 / n) × R^(2/3) × S^(1/2), solved for the self-cleansing slope at the entered scour velocity (2 ft/s if blank) and the slope to carry target flow at half-full with R = D / 4.
manning-slope.edition: Manning equation; closed-conduit n-values are the 'normal' values of Chow, Open-Channel Hydraulics (1959) Table 5-6 (copper 0.011, coated cast iron 0.013, galvanized 0.016, corrugated storm drain 0.024), by name; PVC 0.009 is the plastic-pipe industry design figure. USGS WSP-2339 covers natural channels and floodplains and was cited here until 2026-10-02 in error.
manning-slope.freeAccess: Chow 1959 at archive.org; the Manning relation is public.
manning-slope.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed plumber / gas fitter govern. Verify against the IPC / IFGC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
manning-slope.editionNote: Single-edition (textbook n-values). The 2 ft/s self-cleansing slope is a velocity criterion only; a sewer design standard can set a higher minimum slope (Ten States Standards 33.41: 0.40% for an 8 in sewer), and the adopted standard governs.

assumptions.name: Half-full hydraulic radius
assumptions.value: R = D / 4

assumptions.name: Self-cleansing velocity
assumptions.value: entered; 2 ft/s if blank (2.5 common, 3.0 on large interceptors)

driveshaft-max-length.formula: N_crit falls as 1/L^2, so L_max = L_ref × sqrt(0.65 × N_crit_ref / target_rpm), keeping the running speed at or below 0.65 × critical. The inverse of N_crit = (4.7/L^2) × sqrt(E I / (rho A)).
driveshaft-max-length.edition: Euler-Bernoulli beam theory by name; AAM (American Axle) and Spicer / Dana driveshaft engineering manuals by name.
driveshaft-max-length.freeAccess: Beam-theory principles free in mechanics-of-materials texts at university OCW.
driveshaft-max-length.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
driveshaft-max-length.editionNote: The longest a driveshaft tube can be before it whips at a target operating speed, the inverse of driveshaft-crit: the first-mode critical speed falls as 1/length^2, so L_max = L_ref × sqrt(0.65 × N_crit_ref / target_rpm), keeping the running speed at or below 0.65 of critical (public guidance is 0.6-0.75). Halving the operating RPM lets the shaft grow by sqrt(2) = 41% before it whips, which is why a long run is split with a center support bearing or built from a larger, stiffer, or composite tube. This is a bare-tube first-mode estimate; the yokes, slip joint, balance, and support bearings shift the real critical speed, so keep margin. Single-edition (physics + manufacturer practice). The driveline manufacturer and a whirl analysis govern.

assumptions.name: 1/L^2 critical speed
assumptions.value: the first-mode critical speed scales as 1/length^2; L_max = L_ref x sqrt(0.65 x N_crit_ref / target_rpm)

assumptions.name: Operating margin
assumptions.value: keeps the running speed at or below 0.65 x critical (guidance 0.6-0.75)

assumptions.name: Bare-tube estimate
assumptions.value: yokes, slip joint, balance, and support bearings shift the real critical speed; keep margin

speaker-impedance.formula: Series Z = sum of Z_i; parallel Z = 1 / sum(1/Z_i) (equal drivers = Z/N); series-parallel combines the two. Safety verdict: total impedance >= amplifier minimum rated load.
speaker-impedance.edition: Ohm's-law series/parallel impedance combination (public); the amplifier-minimum-load check follows the manufacturer's rated minimum, by name (user-supplied).
speaker-impedance.freeAccess: Public Ohm's-law network theory. The amplifier specification governs the rated minimum load.
speaker-impedance.governance: Estimate. Head rigger and manufacturer working-load-limit charts govern. Inspect every piece of hardware before the show.
speaker-impedance.editionNote: Single-edition (physics). A nominal-impedance estimate; real loudspeaker impedance is frequency-dependent, and the amp's spec governs.

assumptions.name: Nominal impedance
assumptions.value: the rated nominal driver impedance, not the frequency-dependent curve

carburetor-altitude-jetting.formula: density ratio = (P / P0) x (T0 / T) on absolute pressure and absolute temperature; jet area ratio = sqrt(density ratio); jet diameter ratio = density ratio ^ 0.25; corrected flow number = original x the area ratio; power ratio is approximately the density ratio.
carburetor-altitude-jetting.edition: The air-density ratio from the absolute pressure ratio times the inverse absolute-temperature ratio, and the carburetor jet-scaling relation in which fuel flow follows jet area times the square root of the venturi depression while required fuel follows air density -- so jet area scales as the square root of the density ratio and jet diameter as its fourth root, by name. A first-order correction for the MAIN circuit only. The engine manufacturer's altitude kit and specifications govern.
carburetor-altitude-jetting.freeAccess: Ratio arithmetic on the user's own pressure, temperature, and jet size; no manufacturer jetting chart is reproduced.
carburetor-altitude-jetting.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
carburetor-altitude-jetting.editionNote: A carburetor is a fixed-geometry device: it meters fuel in proportion to the airflow through the venturi and it was calibrated for one air density. Take it up a mountain and the air thins while the fuel metering does not, so the mixture goes rich, and rich costs power on top of the power already lost to the thin air, fouls plugs, and on a two-stroke can load up badly enough to stall. Temperature matters as much as pressure and pulls the other way, because cold air is dense, so a cold morning at altitude leans out less than a hot afternoon at the same elevation; both terms are in the ratio. The part that is easy to get backward is which quantity the ratio applies to. Fuel flow through a jet goes as its area times the square root of the venturi depression, and the depression itself falls with air density, so delivering fuel in proportion to density requires the jet AREA to scale as the square root of the density ratio and the jet DIAMETER as its fourth root. That is also what the published altitude jetting charts do, and it is why a diameter-measured jet looks deceptively insensitive: the correct change at eight thousand feet is less than four thousandths of an inch, so those jets get under-corrected in the field. Power falls roughly with the density ratio, which matches the familiar rule of about three percent per thousand feet. This is a first-order correction for the main circuit only; idle, pilot, and needle circuits have their own calibration and their own altitude behavior.

assumptions.name: Area is the square root
assumptions.value: fuel flow goes as area x sqrt(depression) and the depression falls with density, so area scales as sqrt(density ratio) and diameter as its fourth root

assumptions.name: Main circuit only
assumptions.value: idle, pilot, and needle circuits have their own calibration; a needle or clip change is often needed alongside

assumptions.name: Invalidated by compensation
assumptions.value: altitude-compensating carburetors, forced induction, and closed-loop control break the whole approach

crane-ground-bearing.formula: gbp = reaction / bearing_area; required_area = reaction / allowable; mat_side = sqrt(required_area); pass = gbp <= allowable.
crane-ground-bearing.edition: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart CC and the manufacturer's outrigger-reaction chart by name; first-principles pressure = force / area.
crane-ground-bearing.freeAccess: OSHA 1926 Subpart CC is free at osha.gov. Allowable soil bearing comes from a geotechnical source.
crane-ground-bearing.governance: Estimate. Head rigger and manufacturer working-load-limit charts govern. Inspect every piece of hardware before the show.
crane-ground-bearing.editionNote: The maximum reaction comes from the outrigger-reaction chart for the lift quadrant, not the static average. Allowable soil bearing must come from a geotech source; voids, backfill, frost, slopes, and adjacent excavations reduce capacity, and a qualified person verifies the setup.

assumptions.name: Pressure
assumptions.value: reaction divided by float / track contact area

assumptions.name: Mat size
assumptions.value: square mat side = sqrt(reaction / allowable)

tagline-force.formula: tag_tension = lateral_force / cos(angle); handlers = ceil(tag_tension / per_person); mechanical_help when tag_tension > 2 x per_person.
tagline-force.edition: OSHA 1926 Subpart CC and standard rigging practice by name; first-principles statics on the tag-line geometry.
tagline-force.freeAccess: OSHA 1926 Subpart CC is free at osha.gov. The geometry is public.
tagline-force.governance: Estimate. Head rigger and manufacturer working-load-limit charts govern. Inspect every piece of hardware before the show.
tagline-force.editionNote: A tag line kept shallow (near horizontal) pulls close to the lateral force it resists; as it steepens toward vertical the tension climbs steeply (T = force / cos of the angle above horizontal), so keep the line low. Tag lines control rotation and position; they do not arrest a falling load. Handlers stand clear of the swing path, and 50 lb sustained per person is a planning default.

assumptions.name: Per-person pull
assumptions.value: 50 lb safe sustained pull per handler (planning default)

asphalt-spread-rate.formula: spread_lb_per_sy = thickness_in x density_pcf x 0.75 (0.75 = 9 sf/sy / 12 in/ft); yield_sy_per_ton = 2000 / spread_lb_per_sy.
asphalt-spread-rate.edition: Asphalt spread / yield identity by name (spread = thickness x density x conversion; yield = 2000 / spread); first-principles unit arithmetic.
asphalt-spread-rate.freeAccess: The spread and yield are public first-principles unit conversions; the compacted density comes from the mix design.
asphalt-spread-rate.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
asphalt-spread-rate.editionNote: The mix design's compacted density governs (typically about 145 pcf for a dense-graded mix). Crews check the roll-ahead yield load by load against the plan: a low yield means the mat is running thick or the trucks are short.

assumptions.name: Density
assumptions.value: compacted HMA density from the mix design, ~145 pcf default for a dense-graded mix

assumptions.name: Conversion
assumptions.value: 0.75 = 9 sf/sy divided by 12 in/ft; yield = 2000 lb/ton / spread

plain-bearing-pressure-pv.formula: P = W/(L D) (projected area); V = pi D N/12 ft/min; PV = P V. Oil-impregnated sintered bronze PV limit ~50,000 psi-ft/min.
plain-bearing-pressure-pv.edition: The plain-bearing projected pressure P = W/(L D), surface velocity V = pi D N/12, and the PV factor with the bearing-material PV limits (Machinery's Handbook), by name; the plain-bearing counterpart to the rolling-bearing rating-life tiles.
plain-bearing-pressure-pv.freeAccess: The projected pressure, surface velocity, and PV factor are standard published plain-bearing results; the load, diameter, length, and speed are the user's inputs, and the rated PV comes from the bushing material.
plain-bearing-pressure-pv.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
plain-bearing-pressure-pv.editionNote: Plain (sleeve/journal) bearing sizing on projected pressure and PV, not rating life. The projected pressure P = W/(L D) uses the projected area L x D (journal diameter D, bearing length L), not the wrapped area; the journal surface velocity is V = pi D N/12 ft/min; and the PV factor is their product, the value that governs the frictional heat and wear. PV must stay under the bearing material's rated limit - roughly 50,000 psi-ft/min for oil-impregnated sintered bronze, higher for pressure-lubricated bronze/babbitt, much lower for dry plastics. Keep the pressure under the material's crush limit and the velocity under its speed limit as well. The hydrodynamic film (Sommerfeld number), the actual temperature rise, minimum film thickness, and the specific material limits are the bushing maker's. Rolling bearings use rating life (bearing-l10-life). A design aid; Machinery's Handbook and the bearing maker govern.

assumptions.name: Projected pressure
assumptions.value: P = W/(L D), projected area L x D not wrapped area

assumptions.name: PV factor
assumptions.value: PV = P V, must stay under the material's rated PV (~50,000 for oil-impregnated bronze)

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: static pressure/PV screen; hydrodynamic film, temperature rise, material limits are the maker's

thread-pitch-dia-from-wires.formula: E = M - 3W + 0.86603 x P, the three-wire relation M = E + 3W - 0.86603 x P solved for the pitch diameter; best wire W = 0.57735 x P (usable range 0.505182P to 1.010362P, ASME B1.2 limits as printed in the Osborn three-wire catalog; 0.650013P is the 29-degree Acme maximum) for a 60-degree thread.
thread-pitch-dia-from-wires.edition: The three-wire measurement-over-wires method for 60-degree threads solved for the pitch diameter, and the best-wire / 0.86603 constant - first-principles geometry as in Machinery's Handbook (Industrial Press), by name; public domain.
thread-pitch-dia-from-wires.freeAccess: Pure geometry, public; compare the resulting pitch diameter E to the thread-class limits for the fit.
thread-pitch-dia-from-wires.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
thread-pitch-dia-from-wires.editionNote: The inverse of thread-measure-wire and the way the method is used on the bench: the machinist reads the measurement M over three wires on the micrometer and wants the pitch diameter E. First-principles 60-degree thread geometry; a wire outside the acceptable range is flagged, not blocked; compare E to the thread-class pitch-diameter limits.

assumptions.name: Thread form
assumptions.value: 60-degree included angle (UN / ISO metric); M is measured over three wires

ellipse-area-perimeter.formula: a = major/2, b = minor/2; area = pi a b (exact); perimeter ~= pi[3(a+b) - sqrt((3a+b)(a+3b))] (Ramanujan); eccentricity = sqrt(1 - (b/a)^2).
ellipse-area-perimeter.edition: The ellipse area pi a b and Ramanujan's perimeter approximation pi[3(a+b) - sqrt((3a+b)(a+3b))] (standard geometry; Ramanujan 1914), by name; public domain.
ellipse-area-perimeter.freeAccess: Pure plane geometry, public; the major and minor axes are user-supplied measurements.
ellipse-area-perimeter.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
ellipse-area-perimeter.editionNote: Area and perimeter of an ellipse from the full major (long) and minor (short) axis lengths, with the semi-axes a = major/2 and b = minor/2. The area is exact, pi a b; the perimeter has no elementary closed form, so this uses Ramanujan's approximation pi[3(a+b) - sqrt((3a+b)(a+3b))], which is within a few parts per million up to about a 2:1 oval and drifts low on flat ones (54 ppm at b/a 0.3, 0.08% at 0.1, 0.34% at 0.01). The eccentricity sqrt(1 - (b/a)^2) (with a the larger semi-axis) measures how far from round it is. When the two axes are equal the ellipse is a circle: the area becomes pi r^2 and the perimeter 2 pi r. Use it for an elliptical bed or border, a running-track lane, an oval tabletop or arch, or an elliptical head footprint. A partial (segment) area, an elliptical tank's partial-fill volume, and a true elliptic-integral perimeter are separate. Plane figure only. A shop and layout aid; verify critical dimensions on the work.

assumptions.name: Area exact
assumptions.value: area = pi a b, a and b the semi-axes

assumptions.name: Ramanujan perimeter
assumptions.value: pi[3(a+b) - sqrt((3a+b)(a+3b))], a few ppm for ordinary ovals; not exact

assumptions.name: Circle limit
assumptions.value: equal axes give a circle (pi r^2, 2 pi r)

gear-identification.formula: Pd = (N + 2)/OD; pitch dia = N/Pd; module = 25.4/Pd; snap Pd to the nearest standard value.
gear-identification.edition: Spur gear identification in the diametral-pitch system (20-degree full-depth involute; Machinery's Handbook / AGMA), the inverse of OD = (N+2)/Pd, by name.
gear-identification.freeAccess: The diametral-pitch tooth proportions and the standard Pd series are standard published gear geometry (Machinery's Handbook).
gear-identification.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
gear-identification.editionNote: Identifying an unknown spur gear from the counted tooth count N and the measured outside (tip) diameter OD, the inverse of the spur-gear-geometry tile. Because OD = (N + 2)/Pd for a standard 20-degree full-depth involute, the diametral pitch is Pd = (N + 2)/OD (teeth per inch), the pitch diameter is N/Pd, and the metric module equivalent is 25.4/Pd. The computed Pd is snapped to the nearest standard diametral pitch so a caliper reading slightly off still identifies the gear; a large percent-off suggests a worn tip, a stub-tooth form, or a metric-module gear measured in inches. This assumes standard full-depth proportions; a stub, high, or nonstandard tooth form shifts the OD-to-Pd relation. A shop aid; confirm against the gear drawing or a gear gauge.

assumptions.name: Pitch from OD
assumptions.value: Pd = (N + 2)/OD for a standard full-depth involute

assumptions.name: Standard-pitch snap
assumptions.value: the measured Pd is matched to the nearest standard diametral pitch for identification

assumptions.name: Tooth form
assumptions.value: assumes 20-deg full-depth proportions; a stub/nonstandard form shifts the relation

ballast-section-volume.formula: bottom width = top + 2 x slope ratio x depth; area = (top + bottom) / 2 x depth; volume cu yd = area x length / 27; tons = volume x placed density; per mile = area x 5,280 / 27; raise volume = top width x raise depth x length / 27.
ballast-section-volume.edition: The trapezoidal prism and a placed-density conversion in tons per cubic yard, by name, as standard track surfacing practice; 27 cubic ft per cubic yard and 5,280 ft per mile are exact. The railroad's standard plans set the section and the supplier's material sets the density.
ballast-section-volume.freeAccess: Prismatic volume arithmetic on the user's own section dimensions and an entered density; no standard plan is reproduced.
ballast-section-volume.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
ballast-section-volume.editionNote: The section is wider at the bottom than at the top because of the side slopes, and on a common slope with a foot of depth that is several extra feet of width -- a large fraction of the total. Computing the section as a rectangle at the top width understates the volume substantially, and the understatement grows with depth, which is why the rectangle comparison is printed alongside the real answer. The distinction that matters on a surfacing job is between the full section and the RAISE. Lifting existing track a couple of inches does not require a new section; it requires the volume of the lift plus what fills the crib and shoulder that the lift opens up. Ordering the full section for a raise buys several times what is needed, and ordering the raise volume for new construction buys a fraction of it. Placed density is the other quiet term. Ballast is bought by the ton and placed by the cubic yard, and the conversion depends on the stone and on compaction, so using loose density rather than placed overstates the yards a ton will cover. This does not deduct the ballast displaced by ties or the crib volume on a raise, it does not handle transitions, turnouts, crossings, bridge approaches, or variable-depth sections, and it does not account for ballast lost into a soft subgrade, which on bad track can consume a large multiple of the calculated volume.

assumptions.name: Side slopes are most of the error
assumptions.value: taking the section off as a rectangle at the top width understates it, and the gap grows with depth

assumptions.name: A raise is not a section
assumptions.value: a surfacing lift needs the lift volume plus crib and shoulder fill, not the full section

assumptions.name: Placed density, not loose
assumptions.value: roughly 1.35 to 1.45 tons per placed cubic yard for typical granite; take it from the supplier's material

hoistway-venting.formula: vent area = hoistway plan area x vent fraction, not less than 3 sq ft per car (the legacy IBC 3004.3 rule); opening force at the knob = closer force + door area x pressure difference x 5.2 lbf per sq ft per in wc x W / (2 (W - d)), the NFPA 92 relation with d the knob distance from the latch edge; supply air = about 2,610 cfm per sq ft of leakage x the square root of the pressure difference in in wc.
hoistway-venting.edition: The historic vent-area fraction and the pressurization orifice relation, by name, with NFPA 92 and the adopted building code named as governing which approach applies. A screen with supporting arithmetic, not a smoke control design.
hoistway-venting.freeAccess: Area and orifice arithmetic on the user's own shaft dimensions and an entered leakage area; no code table is reproduced.
hoistway-venting.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
hoistway-venting.editionNote: The two approaches solve the same problem in opposite directions and the code has moved. Venting accepts that smoke enters the shaft and gives it somewhere to go; pressurization supplies air to the shaft to keep smoke out in the first place. Energy codes disliked permanent open vents at the top of every hoistway, and smoke control practice preferred keeping the shaft clean, so pressurization became the common answer -- but which is required depends entirely on the adopted code and the authority having jurisdiction, and buildings exist with both. The constraint that bounds pressurization is the door: too little pressure and smoke migrates in, too much and the pressure difference across the hoistway and stairwell doors makes them hard to open, which fails the egress force limits. That band is narrow, and it is narrower in tall buildings where the shaft's own stack effect adds a season-dependent pressure the fan has to work with rather than against, and which reverses between summer and winter, so a system commissioned in one season can behave quite differently in the other. The interaction with the elevator matters too: cars used for occupant evacuation or firefighter operations carry additional requirements, and what the pressurization system does when a door opens is what a commissioning test has to demonstrate.

assumptions.name: Which approach applies is a code question
assumptions.value: vent, pressurize, or neither is set by the adopted edition and the authority having jurisdiction

assumptions.name: The door sets the ceiling
assumptions.value: pressure difference across the door must stay inside the egress opening-force limit

assumptions.name: Stack effect is larger than the band
assumptions.value: and it reverses with the season, so commissioning in one season proves little about the other

max-circuit-length-for-vd.formula: vd_target_volts = target_vd_pct/100 x source_voltage_v; max_length_ft = vd_target_volts x conductor_cmil / (factor x k_constant x current_a), factor = 2 single-phase / sqrt(3) three-phase, K = 12.9 Cu / 21.2 Al ohm-cmil/ft.
max-circuit-length-for-vd.edition: First-principles I x R voltage drop solved for length (public); the NEC 210.19 / 215.2 3% branch / 5% total figures are informational recommendations, not requirements; the AHJ and the adopted NEC edition govern.
max-circuit-length-for-vd.freeAccess: The voltage-drop length relation is public Ohm's law; the target percent, current, conductor circular mils, and material constant are the circuit and conductor values.
max-circuit-length-for-vd.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
max-circuit-length-for-vd.editionNote: The maximum one-way circuit length that keeps the voltage drop at or below a chosen target -- the field question 'how far can I run this wire?' It is the standard I x R voltage-drop relation solved for length. The drop over a run is VD = (2 for single-phase, sqrt(3) for three-phase) x K x I x L / cmil, where K is the conductor's resistivity constant in ohm-circular-mils per foot (12.9 for copper, 21.2 for aluminum, at about 75 C), I is the load current, L the one-way length, and cmil the conductor's circular-mil cross-sectional area. Setting VD equal to the allowable drop -- the target percent times the source voltage -- and solving gives L = VD_target x cmil / (factor x K x I). A #12 copper conductor (6,530 circular mils) carrying 20 A on a 120 V single-phase branch reaches about 45 feet before its drop hits 3%; the identical wire on a 208 V three-phase circuit reaches about 91 feet, because the three-phase factor sqrt(3) is smaller than the single-phase 2 and the higher voltage allows more volts of drop for the same percentage. The length scales inversely with current (doubling the load halves the reach), directly with the conductor area (a bigger wire runs farther), and with the source voltage. Two important limits: this accounts for DC resistance only, so on larger conductors and at a lagging power factor the AC reactance adds to the drop (use voltage-drop-reactance for that), and the familiar 3% branch / 5% total figures are informational recommendations in NEC 210.19 and 215.2, not enforceable limits. Separately, the conductor selected for length must still satisfy the NEC 310.16 ampacity and the termination-temperature rules on its own. A design aid; the AHJ and the adopted NEC edition govern.

assumptions.name: I x R solved for length
assumptions.value: L = VD_target x cmil / (factor x K x I); factor 2 single-phase / sqrt(3) three-phase; K 12.9 Cu / 21.2 Al; VD_target = target% x source V

assumptions.name: Limits
assumptions.value: DC-resistance only (reactance adds on large conductors, see voltage-drop-reactance); 3%/5% are NEC recommendations; the conductor must still pass the 310.16 ampacity check

stair-code-check.formula: IBC (commercial): riser 4-7 in, tread >= 11 in, width >= 44 in (36 in where the occupant load is under 50). IRC (residential): riser <= 7.75 in, tread >= 10 in, width >= 36 in. Each measured value is compared to its limit; 2R + T (comfort 24-25 in) is reported, not enforced.
stair-code-check.edition: IBC 2021 (International Building Code) §1011.5.2 (riser/tread) and §1011.2 (width), and IRC 2021 (International Residential Code) R311.7.5 (riser/tread) and R311.7.1 (width), by section; dimensional minimums only, not reproduced.
stair-code-check.freeAccess: Read-only at codes.iccsafe.org. The dimensional stair limits are facts; the AHJ-adopted code and edition govern.
stair-code-check.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed structural engineer govern.
stair-code-check.editionNote: Multi-edition (the AHJ-adopted IBC / IRC edition governs the riser, tread, and width minimums). IBC 2021 §1011.5.2 caps the commercial riser at 7 in (4 in minimum) and floors the tread at 11 in; §1011.2 requires 44 in of width (36 in where the occupant load is under 50). IRC 2021 R311.7.5 allows a 7-3/4 in residential riser and a 10 in tread; R311.7.1 requires 36 in of width. The tread is the horizontal run excluding the nosing; 2R + T of 24-25 in is a comfort rule of thumb, not a code pass/fail. The 3/8 in riser/tread uniformity limit over a flight, the nosing profile, the landings, and winder/spiral geometry are separate checks; the egress width the occupant load requires is the egress-capacity tile.

assumptions.name: Thresholds
assumptions.value: IBC commercial riser 4-7 in, tread 11 in min, width 44 in (36 in where the occupant load is under 50); IRC residential riser 7-3/4 in max, tread 10 in min, width 36 in

assumptions.name: Comfort read
assumptions.value: 2R + T between 24 and 25 in is a design rule of thumb reported for reference, not a code pass/fail requirement

assumptions.name: Separate checks
assumptions.value: the 3/8 in flight uniformity limit, nosing, landings, winders, and the occupant-load egress width (the egress-capacity tile) are not checked here; the AHJ governs

wind-velocity-pressure-exposure-coeffici.formula: Kz = 2.41 (z/zg)^(2/alpha) for 15 ft <= z <= zg; Kz = 2.41 (15/zg)^(2/alpha) for z < 15 ft. ASCE 7-22 Table 26.11-1: B alpha 7.5 zg 3280, C 9.8/2460, D 11.5/1935.
wind-velocity-pressure-exposure-coeffici.edition: The ASCE 7-22 §26.10.1 velocity pressure exposure coefficient Kz (Table 26.10-1), with the revised Table 26.11-1 terrain exposure constants (alpha, zg), by name.
wind-velocity-pressure-exposure-coeffici.freeAccess: ASCE 7 is available through the ASCE Library at ascelibrary.org; the §26.10 exposure-coefficient equation and the Table 26.11-1 constants are public. The height z is the user's own building dimension.
wind-velocity-pressure-exposure-coeffici.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
wind-velocity-pressure-exposure-coeffici.editionNote: The ASCE 7-22 §26.10.1 velocity pressure exposure coefficient Kz, the height- and exposure-dependent factor the wind-pressure and wind-cc-pressure tiles take as an input but only stub with a flat 30 ft value. Kz = 2.41 (z/zg)^(2/alpha) for 15 ft <= z <= the gradient height zg, held at the z = 15 ft value below 15 ft, with the 7-22 Table 26.11-1 constants alpha and zg by exposure (B 7.5/3280 ft, C 9.8/2460 ft, D 11.5/1935 ft). ASCE 7-16 used 2.01 with B 7.0/1200, C 9.5/900, D 11.5/700 ft, which runs up to about 4% higher aloft (B at 100 ft: 0.99 against 0.95). It scales the velocity pressure qz = 0.00256 Kz Kzt Ke V^2 (7-22 applies Kd in the pressure equations instead), so it rises with height and with a smoother exposure. At 30 ft it returns 0.69 (B), 0.98 (C), and 1.17 (D), within 0.01 of the values the tiles hard-code, while a 50 ft eave in Exposure C is 1.09, about 11% more pressure. Kz is used at each height z for the windward wall and Kh (Kz at the mean roof height) for the leeward, side, and roof surfaces and for all components and cladding. Above the gradient height the tabulated range ends. A design aid, not a substitute for the structural engineer of record.

assumptions.name: Exposure coefficient
assumptions.value: Kz = 2.41 (z/zg)^(2/alpha), held at the z = 15 ft value below 15 ft

assumptions.name: Use
assumptions.value: Kz per height z for windward, Kh (mean roof height) for leeward/side/roof and all C&C

steel-effective-length-k.formula: G = sum(EI/L)_columns / sum(EI/L)_beams; sway: K = sqrt((1.6 GA GB + 4(GA+GB) + 7.5)/(GA+GB+7.5)); braced: K = (3 GA GB + 1.4(GA+GB) + 0.64)/(3 GA GB + 2(GA+GB) + 1.28).
steel-effective-length-k.edition: The AISC alignment-chart effective-length factor K from the joint stiffness ratios G, via the Dumonteil closed-form approximations to the sway and braced nomographs, by name.
steel-effective-length-k.freeAccess: The AISC alignment charts and the Dumonteil closed-form fits are public results in the AISC Commentary and the standard steel-design references.
steel-effective-length-k.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
steel-effective-length-k.editionNote: The AISC alignment-chart stiffness ratio G = sum(EI/L)_columns / sum(EI/L)_beams, the Dumonteil sway approximation K = sqrt((1.6 GA GB + 4(GA+GB) + 7.5)/(GA+GB+7.5)) and braced approximation K = (3 GA GB + 1.4(GA+GB) + 0.64)/(3 GA GB + 2(GA+GB) + 1.28), and the recommended G = 10 (pinned) / G = 1 (fixed) end conditions. This returns the effective-length factor from the joint stiffness ratios - it uses the Dumonteil closed-form fits (within ~2% of the nomograph), assumes the chart's idealizing assumptions (elastic behavior, all columns buckling simultaneously, equal L/r), and does not compute the G factors from member sizes for the user or apply the inelastic stiffness-reduction tau_b. A design aid, not a substitute for the structural engineer of record's stamped design.

assumptions.name: Stiffness ratio
assumptions.value: G = sum(EI/L)_columns / sum(EI/L)_beams at each joint (10 pinned, 1 fixed)

assumptions.name: Closed-form K
assumptions.value: the Dumonteil sway/braced fits, within ~2% of the nomograph

assumptions.name: Chart assumptions
assumptions.value: elastic behavior, simultaneous column buckling, equal L/r; no tau_b

wood-nail-withdrawal.formula: W = 1,380 G^(5/2) D (lb/in); Ctn = toenailed ? 0.67 : 1.0; CM = 1.0, or 0.25 when the wood's moisture changes after nailing (NDS Table 11.3.3); Z_w = W x p x CD x CM x Ctn.
wood-nail-withdrawal.edition: The NDS 2018 12.2.3 reference nail/spike withdrawal design value and the toenail factor, by name; the 1,380 empirical constant is named.
wood-nail-withdrawal.freeAccess: The NDS is free to view at awc.org (ANSI/AWC NDS); the 12.2.3 withdrawal equation and the 12.5.4 toenail factor are in the published standard.
wood-nail-withdrawal.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
wood-nail-withdrawal.editionNote: The NDS 2018 12.2.3 reference withdrawal W = 1,380 G^(5/2) D (lb/in) with G the holding member's specific gravity and D the fastener diameter, the capacity W x p_pen, the toenail factor Ctn = 0.67 (12.5.4), the wet service factor CM (Table 11.3.3: 0.25 when nails are driven in green lumber that then dries, or in dry lumber that then gets wet), and the rule that withdrawal from end grain is not permitted (12.2.3.4). This returns the reference nail-withdrawal design value and capacity - it applies to a nail loaded in withdrawal from side grain (not end grain), uses the holding member's specific gravity, multiplies by the entered CD, CM, and Ctn, and does not cover lateral (shear) loading, the head pull-through, or combined withdrawal-plus-lateral. A design aid, not a substitute for the structural engineer of record's stamped design.

assumptions.name: Withdrawal value
assumptions.value: W = 1,380 G^(5/2) D per inch of penetration into the holding member

assumptions.name: Toenail factor
assumptions.value: Ctn = 0.67 for a toenailed connection (12.5.4)

assumptions.name: Side grain only
assumptions.value: withdrawal from end grain is not permitted

outside-air-percent-temps.edition: The mixed-air temperature balance for the outside-air fraction from ASHRAE / AABC-NEBB field practice, by name.
outside-air-percent-temps.freeAccess: The mixed-air temperature-balance outside-air percentage is a standard published air-balancing field check.
outside-air-percent-temps.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
outside-air-percent-temps.editionNote: The measured outside-air fraction from a mixed-air temperature balance: %OA = 100 (T_ra - T_ma) / (T_ra - T_oa). The mixed-air temperature is the flow-weighted blend of return and outside air, so its position between the two reads the damper's actual outside-air fraction, the field check against the design minimum ventilation. It needs well-mixed, shielded dry-bulb readings; a mixed-air temperature outside the return/outdoor band signals a stratified duct or a sensor fault, and a return-to-outdoor spread under about 10 F makes the percentage sensitive to sensor error. A field aid, not a substitute for a direct airflow measurement.

assumptions.name: Temperature balance
assumptions.value: %OA = 100 (T_ra - T_ma) / (T_ra - T_oa)

assumptions.name: Well-mixed readings
assumptions.value: shielded dry-bulb sensors in well-mixed air

assumptions.name: Low-spread caveat
assumptions.value: a return-to-outdoor spread under ~10 F is sensitive to sensor error

slip-critical-with-tension.formula: ksc = 1 - Tu/(Du Tb nb) (Eq. J3-5a, LRFD), floored at 0; reduced slip resistance = ksc x Rn where Rn = mu Du hf Tb ns; LRFD phi = 1.00; ASD uses its own ksc = 1 - 1.5 Ta/(Du Tb nb) (Eq. J3-5b, the entered tension read as the service-level Ta), floored at 0, with Omega = 1.50; standard holes.
slip-critical-with-tension.edition: AISC 360 Section J3.9, slip-critical connections subject to combined tension and shear, by section number; the unreduced resistance comes from this catalog's landed slip-critical tile rather than being recomputed.
slip-critical-with-tension.freeAccess: AISC 360 is available through AISC; the J3.9 interaction expression is a published code equation.
slip-critical-with-tension.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed structural engineer govern.
slip-critical-with-tension.editionNote: Applied tension relieves part of the clamping force a slip-critical joint runs on, so the slip resistance is scaled by ksc. Note the denominator uses Du Tb - the MEAN installed pretension, not the specified minimum - because the reduction is measured against the pretension actually present, which is why Du appears here as well as in the base resistance. Past Tu = Du Tb nb the factor reaches zero and the joint has NO slip resistance left: the bolts may be intact but the faying surfaces are free to move. THIS IS THE SLIP CHECK ONLY, and slip is a SERVICEABILITY limit - the strength-level bolt shear and bearing check (bolt-shear-bearing) and the J3.7 combined tension-shear rupture check (steel-bolt-tension-shear) are separate, and a joint can pass all three or fail any one independently. Prying action increases the tension the bolts actually see beyond the applied load and is NOT modeled here (bolt-prying-action computes it); it matters most on thin end plates and tees. Standard holes assumed. AISC 360 and the engineer of record govern.

assumptions.name: ksc interaction
assumptions.value: LRFD 1 - Tu/(Du Tb nb); ASD 1 - 1.5 Ta/(Du Tb nb); each floored at zero

assumptions.name: Mean pretension
assumptions.value: Du Tb, not the specified minimum, is the clamping force the tension is measured against

assumptions.name: Slip only
assumptions.value: serviceability limit; shear/bearing and J3.7 rupture are separate checks

assumptions.name: No prying
assumptions.value: prying action raises the actual bolt tension and is not modeled

economizer-enthalpy-changeover.formula: differential enthalpy: enable unless h_outdoor > h_return; fixed dry-bulb: enable unless t_outdoor > setpoint; differential enthalpy + fixed dry-bulb (90.1-2013+): enable unless h_outdoor > h_return or t_outdoor > the entered fixed dry-bulb limit (75 F under 90.1-2013+ Table 6.5.1.1.3); margin = the difference to the binding limit.
economizer-enthalpy-changeover.edition: The air-side economizer high-limit (changeover) control, differential enthalpy and fixed dry-bulb, from ASHRAE 90.1 6.5.1.1.3, by name.
economizer-enthalpy-changeover.freeAccess: The differential-enthalpy and fixed-dry-bulb high-limit logic is the published ASHRAE 90.1 economizer control requirement.
economizer-enthalpy-changeover.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
economizer-enthalpy-changeover.editionNote: The air-side economizer high-limit (changeover) control per ASHRAE 90.1 Table 6.5.1.1.3. In differential-enthalpy mode the economizer is enabled (free cooling) when the outdoor-air total heat content (enthalpy) is below the return-air enthalpy and locked out above it, which correctly rejects a cool but humid outdoor condition that carries more total energy than the return (bringing it in would add a dehumidification load). In fixed-dry-bulb mode it is enabled below a dry-bulb setpoint (commonly 65-75 F by climate zone) and locked out above; this is simpler but ignores humidity. Since 90.1-2013 the prescriptive enthalpy option is differential enthalpy WITH a fixed dry-bulb limit (the third mode), which also locks out a hot, dry day whose enthalpy is below the return. This returns the enable/lock-out decision and the margin to the changeover; it does not model the mixed-air reset, the minimum-position damper, or the actual free-cooling energy (see economizer-savings-hours). A control aid; the ASHRAE 90.1 high-limit for the climate zone and the equipment control sequence govern.

assumptions.name: Differential enthalpy
assumptions.value: enable unless h_outdoor > h_return (accounts for latent load)

assumptions.name: Fixed dry-bulb
assumptions.value: enable below a dry-bulb setpoint (climate-zone dependent)

assumptions.name: Combined (90.1-2013+)
assumptions.value: differential enthalpy with fixed dry-bulb: shut off if hOA > hRA or TOA > 75 F (all zones); plain differential enthalpy left the prescriptive table in 2013

assumptions.name: Decision only
assumptions.value: does not model reset, minimum position, or free-cooling energy

ceiling-water-load.formula: load_psf = (avg_depth_in/12) x 62.4; weight_lb = pooled_area_ft2 x (avg_depth_in/12) x 62.4 = volume_gal x 8.34; volume_gal = pooled_area_ft2 x (avg_depth_in/12) x 7.48052; drain_first = load_psf > threshold_psf.
ceiling-water-load.edition: Hydrostatic load and water density (62.4 lb/ft^3, 8.34 lb/gal, 7.48052 gal/ft^3) by name; ANSI/IICRC S500 safety practice. Not edition-bound.
ceiling-water-load.freeAccess: Water is ~62.4 lb/ft^3, so a foot of depth is 62.4 psf and an inch is 5.2 psf. The densities are public constants.
ceiling-water-load.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
ceiling-water-load.editionNote: Single-edition (the water densities and the hydrostatic load do not roll). The drain-first threshold is an EDITABLE screen value, NOT a code capacity - the actual fastening, span, and a structural engineer govern. This screens whether to punch-drain from a safe distance before working beneath the bulge.

assumptions.name: Threshold
assumptions.value: the drain-first load (default 5 psf) is an editable, conservative screen, not a structural rating

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: a safety screen for trapped overhead water; the wet gypsum's fastening and a structural engineer govern collapse

flat-surface-heat-loss.formula: Air at the film temperature (Sutherland mu and k, ideal-gas density, cp 1,006 J/kg K); Ra = g (1/Tf) |Ts - Ta| L^3/(nu alpha). Vertical (L = height): Nu = 0.68 + 0.670 Ra^(1/4)/[1 + (0.492/Pr)^(9/16)]^(4/9) to Ra 1e9, else [0.825 + 0.387 Ra^(1/6)/(1 + (0.492/Pr)^(9/16))^(8/27)]^2. Horizontal (L = area/perimeter): hot side up or cold side down Nu = 0.54 Ra^(1/4) to Ra 1e7, else 0.15 Ra^(1/3); hot side down or cold side up Nu = 0.27 Ra^(1/4). h_rad = eps sigma (Ts^4 - Ta^4)/(Ts - Ta), sigma = 0.1714e-8 BTU/hr ft2 R4; q = (h_conv + h_rad) A (Ts - Ta).
flat-surface-heat-loss.edition: Free convection from flat plates as given in Incropera, DeWitt, Bergman and Lavine, Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, Ch. 9 (Churchill and Chu 1975 for the vertical plate; McAdams for the horizontal plate), and gray-body radiation to large surroundings, by name.
flat-surface-heat-loss.freeAccess: Standard heat-transfer correlations; checked against the textbook's Example 9.3 (a 0.75 by 0.3 m duct at 45 C in 15 C air: sides 4.23, top 5.47, bottom 2.07 W/m2 K), reproduced within 1%.
flat-surface-heat-loss.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
flat-surface-heat-loss.editionNote: Heat loss from a bare flat surface to still air. A hot surface facing up (or a cold one facing down) is buoyancy-assisted and convects about two and a half times as fast as the same surface facing the other way. Radiation is usually half or more of the loss. The combined coefficient is the outer film the insulation calculators take as entered. Valid to Ra 1e13; wind and forced convection are not included.

assumptions.name: Characteristic length
assumptions.value: height for a vertical plate; area over perimeter for a horizontal one

assumptions.name: Radiation
assumptions.value: gray surface to large surroundings at the air temperature

assumptions.name: Still air
assumptions.value: no wind or forced convection; the surface temperature is uniform

pig-batch-volume.formula: line volume V = (pi/4) d^2 L converted at 42 gallons of 231 cubic inches per barrel; pig velocity = flow / volume per unit length; travel time = length / velocity; and the flow that reaches a target velocity is that relation inverted.
pig-batch-volume.edition: The geometry of a cylinder with the exact petroleum-barrel conversion, and pig velocity as flow over area. The inline inspection tool's velocity window is ENTERED from the vendor's specification. It assumes a constant inside diameter and a full line, and does not model bypass around the pig, the differential pressure driving it, tool wear, or the batch interface mixing length.
pig-batch-volume.freeAccess: One cylinder volume and one exact unit conversion.
pig-batch-volume.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pig-batch-volume.editionNote: A pipeline is a very long cylinder and its volume is larger than intuition suggests -- the number that sizes the receiver, the tankage and the displacement batch at once. Velocity matters for more than scheduling: too slow and a cleaning pig can stall or its bypass lets debris past, too fast and an inspection tool's sensors cannot sample properly and the run has to be repeated. The window check is therefore reported as a verdict COMPUTED from the velocity, naming which end was missed and the throughput that would fix it, because a velocity a little under a minimum reads as acceptable at a glance and is not.

assumptions.name: Constant inside diameter
assumptions.value: a real line has fittings, bends and diameter changes

assumptions.name: The tool window is entered
assumptions.value: every tool has its own specification

assumptions.name: No bypass model
assumptions.value: a cleaning pig's bypass changes both velocity and cleaning

secondary-glycol-loop.formula: water-basis flow = Q / (500 x dT); the fluid factor is 500 x specific gravity x specific heat and the corrected flow is Q / (fluid factor x dT); pump bhp = gpm x head x specific gravity / (3,960 x efficiency); the temperature penalty is the chiller approach plus the coil approach, times the entered percent per degF.
secondary-glycol-loop.edition: The water-side transport relation with the SG x cp correction for a secondary fluid, and pump brake horsepower as pump practice writes it. The 500 constant is 8.33 lb/gal x 60 min/h x water's specific heat of 1.0, and 3,960 is 33,000 ft-lb/min per hp over that same water basis. Fluid properties, head and the approach temperatures are ENTERED. It does not compute viscosity or pressure drop, size the pump or chiller, or set freeze protection.
secondary-glycol-loop.freeAccess: Two flow relations and one pump relation; no proprietary fluid data is reproduced.
secondary-glycol-loop.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
secondary-glycol-loop.editionNote: The flow correction is the part that gets skipped. The familiar 500 constant is water's number, and because a glycol solution's SG x cp product is below one the same duty at the same delta-T needs MORE flow, not less. The fluid factor reported here is exactly the input hydronic-gpm-deltat asks the user to supply, so this computes what that tile takes on faith. The temperature penalty compounds separately: a glycol coil sees fluid warmer than the refrigerant by the chiller's approach, so the evaporator runs colder for the same room, and every degree is compressor power. That is the honest price of the charge reduction a secondary loop buys.

assumptions.name: Fluid properties are entered
assumptions.value: specific heat and specific gravity vary with glycol type, concentration and temperature

assumptions.name: Head is entered
assumptions.value: viscosity at low temperature raises it substantially and is not computed here

assumptions.name: The compressor sensitivity is entered
assumptions.value: it depends on refrigerant, suction condition and machine

crown-reduction-leaf-area.formula: crown projection area = pi/4 x diameter squared, so it goes as the SQUARE of the radius; leaf area is distributed by radial shell with the entered majority share in the outer third of the radius, and the reduction removes the outer shell first; the reduction that just reaches the dose cap is that relation bisected.
crown-reduction-leaf-area.edition: The crown projection and leaf-area distribution relations by name, checked against the ANSI A300 live crown removal dose -- about 25% of the live crown in a season for a mature tree, less for young, over-mature and stressed trees. The outer-third share is ENTERED: it varies by species, age, light exposure and prior management. A geometric estimate on a circular crown projection; it does not measure leaf area, select cuts, or assess the tree. ANSI A300 Part 1, the ISA Best Management Practices, and a qualified arborist govern.
crown-reduction-leaf-area.freeAccess: Two areas and a share the reader supplies; no A300 text is reproduced.
crown-reduction-leaf-area.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
crown-reduction-leaf-area.editionNote: The geometry compounds twice. Crown projection goes as the SQUARE of the radius, so taking a fifth off the radius takes over a third of the projected area -- and LEAVES ARE ON THE OUTSIDE, so the shell that cut removes is the densest part of the crown. A reduction described as a few feet off the ends can therefore remove far more leaf area than the feet suggest, and the amplification between the two is the figure a client and an arborist argue about. Heavy reduction triggers epicormic sprouting -- weakly attached shoots that must be managed for years -- and topping is not pruning at all: it removes leaf area indiscriminately and creates a decay entry at every cut.

assumptions.name: The outer-third share is entered
assumptions.value: it varies by species, age, light exposure and prior management

assumptions.name: A circular projection in radial shells
assumptions.value: no real crown is that, and leaf area is not measured here

assumptions.name: It does not select cuts
assumptions.value: a reduction is made to laterals large enough to assume the terminal role

safe-room-capacity.formula: usable area = gross x (1 - 0.50, 0.35, or 0.15) or the entered net area; community rooms: the largest total T with (T - W - B) x standing + W x wheelchair + B x bed <= usable area, W = ceil(T / 200); residential rooms: floor(usable area / density), routed to the community criteria above 16 occupants.
safe-room-capacity.edition: FEMA P-361, Safe Rooms for Tornadoes and Hurricanes, Part B, Section B5.2.1: Table B5-1 (community tornado 5 / 10 / 30 sq ft), Table B5-2 (community hurricane 20 / 20 / 40), Table B5-3 (residential tornado 3 or 5, hurricane 7 or 10), one wheelchair space per 200 occupants, and the 50% / 35% / 15% usable-area reductions, with ICC 500 Sections 502 and 503 cited by number. The safe room designer and the AHJ govern.
safe-room-capacity.freeAccess: FEMA P-361 is a free federal publication; the densities and reductions are also printed in FEMA's Safe Room Technical Review job aid. No ICC 500 text is reproduced.
safe-room-capacity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
safe-room-capacity.editionNote: Occupant density is set by how long people will be inside: a tornado passes in minutes and a hurricane lasts a day or more, so the same room holds about a quarter as many for a hurricane. The wheelchair rule couples the count to itself -- every 200 occupants or portion thereof need a wheelchair space at the wheelchair density -- so the tile solves for the largest total that fits, which reproduces FEMA's 4,800 sq ft classroom at 955 occupants rather than 960. Hurricane safe rooms may not count restroom area; tornado rooms may count restroom area outside the stalls only under P-361's conditions. Capacity is not qualification: the structure, siting, and ventilation are separate ICC 500 and P-361 requirements, and code occupant loads for normal use are posted alongside.

assumptions.name: Community densities
assumptions.value: tornado 5 / 10 / 30 sq ft, hurricane 20 / 20 / 40 sq ft (standing, wheelchair, bed)
assumptions.source: FEMA P-361 Tables B5-1 and B5-2; FEMA Safe Room Technical Review (2022)

assumptions.name: One wheelchair space per 200 occupants
assumptions.value: or portion thereof, in community safe rooms

assumptions.name: Usable area reductions
assumptions.value: at least 50% concentrated or fixed seating, 35% unconcentrated, 15% open plan
assumptions.source: FEMA P-361 Section B5.2.1; FEMA Safe Room Technical Review (2022)
